summary: This informational document describes features and use cases of an MPLS path monitoring system. Segment-based routing offers a scalable and simple way to check the liveness of all the paths in one domain. The system adds features to traditional MPLS monitoring.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how a monitoring system can test MPLS paths by sending probes through the data plane. Comparing probes that take slightly different routes can help locate a faulty link.

questions: how to monitor mpls data plane liveness

how does segment routing help mpls monitoring
subtitle: A topology-aware system that sends probes along chosen MPLS paths and checks their return.

tldr.problem: Operators need to test actual MPLS forwarding paths and locate faults without relying on control-plane signaling for every probe.
tldr.mechanism: A Path Monitoring System learns the IGP and MPLS topology, builds a segment label stack, and sends an OAM probe out along the path and back to itself.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8403 is an Informational description of a system and use cases that reuse existing OAM protocols; it defines no new protocol.

facts.label: Example ping stack size
facts.value: No more than 3 labels in the described use case

today: RFC 8403 is an Informational document published in July 2018. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the system reuses existing OAM protocols.

sections.title: A Topology-Aware Monitoring System
sections.content:
Operators need to test the forwarding paths that carry user packets. Segment Routing lets a monitoring packet follow predefined segments through the data plane.

The Path Monitoring System (PMS) described here is limited to one IGP MPLS domain and can monitor SR paths as well as non-SR LSPs such as LDP. It learns topology, sends OAM probes, and receives them back; the system may be physical or virtual.
sections.plainLanguage: The PMS uses network topology information to send test packets along paths that carry user traffic. It checks whether those packets return to the monitoring system.

sections.title: Building and Returning a Probe
sections.content:
The PMS learns the IGP Link State Database, including segment identifiers, and builds an MPLS label stack. The stack can send a probe from the PMS to a starting router, along the path being tested, and then back to the PMS.

The probe may use ICMP, BFD, Seamless BFD, MPLS LSP ping, or another OAM format supported by the PMS. If the probe returns and no IGP change is detected, the path can be treated as validated for continuity.
sections.plainLanguage: The PMS writes the route into the probe's label stack. The packet travels to the path under test and then returns to the PMS.

sections.title: Monitoring Paths and Localizing Faults
sections.content:
In one example, the RFC assigns Node-SIDs to the PMS and two edge routers. A label stack of 20 - 30 - 10 sends a probe from the PMS to LER i, then to LER j, and back to the PMS. A preliminary MPLS path trace can help select an IP destination that follows a particular ECMP path.

For a bundle of links, the PMS can create probes whose segment lists differ at one adjacency. If one probe succeeds and another fails, their difference can point to a link direction with a forwarding problem. The RFC notes that real deployments need careful engineering for unambiguous diagnosis.
sections.plainLanguage: Probes can test a chosen path or different links in a bundle. Comparing which probes return can help narrow down where forwarding fails.

sections.title: Continuity Versus Connectivity Verification
sections.content:
A probe that returns shows continuity, but it may have followed an unintended path if a forwarding entry is wrong. For connectivity verification, the PMS can send a probe with a short TTL at a selected segment so the expected router must respond.

The PMS can also use SR to reach and leave non-SR LDP or RSVP-TE paths, but it needs another way to learn their topology. It must keep topology information current so monitoring packets do not use stale labels.
sections.plainLanguage: A returning probe does not always prove that it used the intended route. A TTL-based check can require a particular router to respond along the way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PMS can insert traffic into non-SR networks, so access must be authorized and should be logged. The RFC suggests reserving service-label ranges and configuring the PMS to reject those labels; IP destinations should be limited to values conforming to RFC 8029.

Stale topology or label information can send probes outside the intended domain. The PMS must follow route changes, stop measurements when relevant topology may be stale, and remove topology information before restarting after a crash.
sections.plainLanguage: A PMS can send packets through the network, so operators must control who can use it. It must also stop using a map when its topology information may be out of date.
